questions.q: What is the general shape of a Snort/Suricata rule?
options: An action, a protocol, a source IP:port, a direction operator, a destination IP:port, and rule options in parentheses
A single keyword with no further structure
A fully compiled binary file
A plain-English sentence with no fixed syntax
questions.explain: Every rule follows the same skeleton: action protocol src_ip src_port -> dst_ip dst_port (rule options).

questions.q: In a rule, what does the action field (such as alert, drop, pass, or reject) control?
options: What the engine does when traffic matches the rule
The source IP address only
The rule's revision number
Whether the rule applies to TCP or UDP traffic
questions.explain: The action field is the very first field in a rule and tells the engine what to do on a match.

questions.q: In the example rule alert tcp any any -> $HOME_NET 80 (msg:"Possible SQL Injection Attempt"; content:"UNION SELECT"; sid:1000001; rev:1;), what does the content option do?
options: Specifies the exact byte pattern — here, the string UNION SELECT — to search for in the packet's payload
Sets the rule's unique identifier
Defines which protocol the rule applies to
Determines the direction of traffic flow
questions.explain: content tells the engine exactly which byte pattern to look for inside the packet's payload.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the sid field in a custom Snort/Suricata rule?
options: It gives the rule a unique numeric ID so it can be referenced unambiguously
It specifies the source IP address being monitored
It determines whether the rule runs in IDS or IPS mode
It is optional and has no functional purpose
questions.explain: Every custom rule needs a unique sid so analysts and tools can reference that exact rule without ambiguity.

questions.q: What does msg:"Possible SQL Injection Attempt" do in a rule?
options: Provides the human-readable description that appears in the alert when the rule fires
Blocks the matching traffic automatically regardless of the action field
Specifies the exact byte pattern to match
Sets the rule's revision number
questions.explain: msg is purely descriptive — it's the text an analyst sees in the alert, not something that changes blocking behavior.
